courses.name: Personal & Professional Development
courses.actualContent: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
courses.contribution: Required PPD

courses.name: Accounting & Corporate Finance
courses.actualContent: This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
courses.contribution: develops accounting and financial-statement analysis for business decisions

courses.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
courses.actualContent: As we enter the “Age of AI,” this course explores AI’s business, managerial, economic, and societal implications. It is designed for UCR students with a strong interest in AI and requires no prior technical background. The course traces AI’s evolution from early research to generative AI, highlighting its capabilities and limits. Through real-world examples and business cases, students analyse AI’s impact on competitiveness, innovation, labour markets, economic growth, inequality, climate change and society. In this context, students critically examine AI governance and ethics, addressing issues such as bias, privacy, and fairness across business functions (e.g. Marketing, HR, Finance), while also exploring corporate governance and regulation more broadly.
courses.contribution: examines managerial, organisational and societal implications of AI and technological change

courses.name: Transnational Business Law
courses.actualContent: This course introduces students to the legal frameworks governing business transactions in a globalized economy. It examines how law shapes cross-border trade, contracts, sales of goods and services, intellectual property, foreign investment, and digital commerce. Emphasis is placed on the practical application of legal rules to real-world business scenarios, as well as on comparative and international perspectives. Through interactive class discussions, problem - based assignments, quizzes, and an arbitration simulation, students develop the analytical and practical skills needed to identify legal risks and design effective solutions in transnational business contexts.
courses.contribution: Direct contribution: transnational contracts, trade, intellectual property, foreign investment and digital commerce address legal aspects of cross-border business; no unestablished company-law coverage is claimed.

courses.name: Money, Banking & Finance
courses.actualContent: This course develops practical financial decision-making skills through case studies and real-world applications. Students learn to analyze financial data, assess risks, and make informed investment, budgeting, and business decisions that enhance value, financial security, and long-term planning.
courses.contribution: develops financial analysis, risk assessment and investment decision-making

courses.name: Introduction to Economics
courses.actualContent: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.
courses.contribution: provides economic foundations on firms, markets, incentives and macroeconomic conditions

courses.name: International Macroeconomics
courses.actualContent: This course explores the economy as a whole by examining its dynamics over the short, medium, and long run. Key indicators such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment are studied. The course analyses how fiscal and monetary polici es affect the economy. It also covers business cycles, economic crises, and international trade, providing the tools needed to interpret economic data, evaluate policy decisions, and understand global economic trends.
courses.contribution: examines growth, inflation, business cycles and policy shaping the international business environment

courses.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
courses.actualContent: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of advanced topics in microeconomic theory. Structured in three parts, the course begins with an in-depth analysis of consumer behaviour, including decision-making under uncertainty, non -egoistic preferences, and cognitive limitations. The second part analyses market structures with an emphasis on imperfect competition, strategic behaviour, and the functioning of factor markets. The final part of the course covers general equilibrium and market efficiency, investigating externalities and the role of government in the economy. Throughout the course, students will engage with research papers through presentations and discussions, bridging theoretical concepts with empirical evidence.
courses.contribution: develops microeconomic and behavioural analysis of consumer and firm decisions

courses.name: Public Economics
courses.actualContent: This course examines the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy affects efficiency and equity. It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.
courses.contribution: Removed from active selections with unsupported third option or replaced communication choice.

courses.name: Econometrics
courses.actualContent: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
courses.contribution: Direct method contribution: OLS, GLS, instrumental variables, statistical tests and an empirical paper support causal and predictive analysis; applications are not restricted to business and the course uses Stata.

courses.name: Behavioral Economics
courses.actualContent: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
courses.contribution: Removed from active selections with unsupported third option or replaced communication choice.

courses.name: Consumer Product Design
courses.actualContent: In this course you will learn how to function in a 'real-world' design and development environment. Hence, you will work in a group that mimics a design and development (d&d) team as e.g. in industry. The members of a team in this course fulfill roles similarly as occur in industrial d&d teams (e.g. chair person, secretary, ...). A team is responsible for much of its own planning. The functioning of a team involves e.g. preparing agendas for team meetings, taking minutes, planning practical work, maintaining a documentation system, etc. During the course, the instructor will NOT act as chairperson / team leader, but rather as an ‘external consultant'. During the course we will go through the various phases of the development of a consumer product: assessment of customer needs and translating these into a product concept, develop a method to make a product, both on laboratory- as on industrial scale, analyzing environmental impact, analyzing costs and proceeds. In a d&d project and hence in the course, activities are quite varied, and include interviewing potential customers, laboratory experiments, constructing quantitative mathematical model(s) of the working mechanism(s) of a product, constructing a prototype, work out how a product can be produced on an industrial scale, consider protection of intellectual property etc.. In this course, in addition to the more traditional aspects of the d&d process, special attention will be given to sustainability. This involves e.g. the nature of the materials used (natural, recycled, …), lifespan, repairability, 'circularity' etc.
courses.contribution: develops product innovation through customer needs, design, costing and team development

courses.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
courses.actualContent: Grounded in academic theory, real-world applications, and case studies, this course unpacks what drives consumers’ behaviour and engagement with brands, and how marketers can build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key concepts related to marketing strategy and consumer psychology and examines external forces influencing reinvention of the Marketing function, including digital and AI-driven marketing. Drawing on the work of Kotler, Aaker, Kapferer and other leading scholars, students will explore real-life case studies, develop marketing plans and learn how to create effective brand strategies for greater consumer engagement.
courses.contribution: examines marketing strategy, consumer psychology and responsible customer engagement

courses.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
courses.actualContent: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
courses.contribution: develops business strategy from vision to execution and responsible digital transformation

courses.name: Market Research
courses.actualContent: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas—perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.
courses.contribution: develops applied business research through data gathering, analysis and managerial recommendations

courses.name: International Business & Governance
courses.actualContent: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
courses.contribution: examines institutions, culture, governance and corporate responsibility in global business

courses.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
courses.actualContent: In this course, you will develop a new venture idea from the ground up. No prior business experience is required – working in teams you will learn by doing, developing a startup concept from ideation through to the final pitch. Along the way, you will gain essential business and entrepreneurial skills, including design thinking, market validation and business planning. This course fosters creativity, business acumen and collaboration to drive business and social entrepreneurship.
courses.contribution: Specific complementary contribution: teamwork, market validation and venture planning apply business strategy and innovation to a new business.

courses.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courses.actualContent: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
courses.contribution: provides research design, surveys, experiments and statistical analysis for management questions

courses.name: Personal Leadership
courses.actualContent: Personal Leadership is an interactive course for Liberal Arts and Sciences students that introduces leadership fundamentals with a focus on self-awareness and practical skills. Through a blend of theory, interaction, and assessments, students will cultivate the tools needed to lead effectively in both personal and professional contexts. The course begins by exploring leadership fundamentals, emphasizing transformational leadership (Bass, 1990) and authentic leadership (Gardner et al., 2021), supported by foundational concepts from Northouse’s Leadership: Theory and Practice (2025), which offers a balanced overview of various leadership models and their applications. Covey’s (2020) The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People: 30th Anniversary Edition provides a foundation for principles such as proactive behavior, prioritization, and fostering collaboration. Students critically analyze these concepts through evolutionary perspectives on adaptive strategies (Lonati & Van Vugt, 2023) and apply Locke and Latham’s (2019) goal-setting theory to develop actionable leadership plans. Self-awareness and emotional intelligence (Goleman, 2021) are central themes, with students engaging in reflective exercises, group discussions, and personality assessments to better understand their strengths, values, and leadership styles. The course maximizes interaction through workshops, group projects, role-playing, and peer feedback sessions, ensuring active engagement and collaboration.
courses.contribution: develops leadership theory, self-awareness and applied leadership practice

courses.name: Leadership Communication
courses.actualContent: Communication and leadership are two sides of the same coin; Quintilian, the famous Roman Professor of Rhetoric, knew this when he famously declared that the best leader is ‘the good person speaking well’. At the start of this course, the participants will be introduced the main leadership and communication models and theories. They will also read leading articles from the Harvard Business Review on leadership communication. Theories that will be explored will include transformational, authentic and adaptive leadership approaches. We will also explore the roles of gender, ethics and culture in communicative leadership positions. The module will focus on the role of emotional intelligence in communicating leadership; touching on key matters such as empathy, ethics, self-awareness and self-regulation. The course will also have a distinctive liberal arts and sciences flavour to it, analysing the leadership qualities and deficiencies of characters in prose fiction, film and drama. It is especially in the worlds created by Shakespeare, where key lessons about how to lead, and how not to lead, can be learned by the leaders of tomorrow. The course will also bring in real leaders from outside the college, from both the business and public sectors, to interact with the students on the subject matter of their own communicative leadership experiences and goals. Such interactions with entrepreneurial and industry heads may lead to spin-off internships in the following academic year.
courses.contribution: Removed from active selections with unsupported third option or replaced communication choice.

courses.name: Leadership & Diversity Management
courses.actualContent: Leadership & Diversity Management explores how diverse perspectives and experiences shape effective leadership in dynamic, varied environments. Blending cutting-edge theories with hands-on practice, students develop the skills to lead with empathy, inclusivity, and adaptability. Through engaging case studies, interactive workshops, and reflective assessments, participants build awareness of diversity and learn to inspire ethical, collaborative teams.
courses.contribution: examines inclusive leadership and diversity management in organisations

courses.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
courses.actualContent: People are the organisation. Without people, organisations cannot survive or be productive. This course, tailored for Liberal Arts and Sciences bachelor students, offers an interdisciplinary exploration of the psychological, social, and structural dynamics within organisations. It equips students with the knowledge and skills needed to navigate and influence organisational environments effectively throughout their academic and professional careers. Drawing on foundational and contemporary research in organisational behaviour, this upper- level undergraduate course incorporates a case-based approach that includes conceptual frameworks, case discussions, and skill-building activities. Students will explore topics such as motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and organizational culture using Robbins and Judge’s (2023) Organisational Behaviour as a primary resource. Additional literature and materials will supplement the course to provide a well-rounded perspective. Topics Covered => Core Concepts: Diversity in organisations, attitudes and job satisfaction, emotions and moods, personality and values, perception and decision-making, motivation, communication, leadership, power and politics, and conflict and negotiation. Structural Dynamics: The structure and culture of organisations, group behaviour, work teams, and organisational change. These topics are structured within a comprehensive model that defines the field of organisational behaviour and outlines its key concepts and relationships.
courses.contribution: examines motivation, groups, organisational culture and structures through organisational psychology

courses.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
courses.actualContent: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence; whether in business, leadership, or life. The course offers an immersive, practice-driven exploration of negotiation as both an analytical discipline and a strategic interpersonal skill. Students will engage in frequent simulations, role-plays, and reflective exercises designed to build confidence and adaptability into the dynamics that shape successful agreements. The course introduces the foundational theories and frameworks that define modern negotiation practice, including BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement), ZOPA analysis (zone of possible agreement), interest-based negotiation, and the dual-concern model. There will also be a focus on (i) avoiding bargaining over positions, (ii) separating people from the problem, (iii) focusing on interests not positions, (iv) inventing options for mutual gain, and (v) insisting on using objective criteria. Students will learn to diagnose negotiation structures, identify value-creation opportunities, and strategically manage trade-offs (e.g. logrolling). Core concepts such as anchoring, framing, concession patterns, and the psychology of influence will be woven throughout weekly activities. Because negotiation is inseparable from human behavior, the course integrates research from social psychology and language & communication studies.
courses.contribution: develops negotiation, strategic interaction and analytical decision-making

courses.name: AI Ethics
courses.actualContent: Developments in AI are transforming the nature of human interaction and raising fundamental questions concerning human flourishing and its alignment with technological progress. This course examines these issues from both philosophical and psychological pe rspectives, while exploring the deep connections between the two fields. In a module on the ethics of AI, we'll consider ramifications of the use of AI in the context of moral inquiry. Core topics include AI fairness and bias , privacy, responsibility and accountability . We will also approach the question concerning the moral status of AI systems , and some of the broader implications of AI, focusing on existential risks and broad political implications of the use of AI. In a module on psychology of AI, we will examine what it means to be human when AI systems increasingly mirror or simulate uniquely human capabilities. Research shows that people may both over-trust and resist AI in decision-making, which subsequently raises questions on responsibility and agency. In clinical and therapeutic contexts, AI challenges ideas of empathy, confidentiality, and the therapeutic alliance, while in organisational and social domains, algorithmic biases reflect and amplify existing stereotypes. Developmentally, AI companions and tutors shape how children learn and relate, prompting concerns about attachment and socialisation.
courses.contribution: examines ethical and societal questions raised by artificial intelligence

courses.name: Decision-making in AI
courses.actualContent: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
courses.contribution: Removed from active selections with unsupported third option or replaced communication choice.

courses.name: Database Management Systems
courses.actualContent: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
courses.contribution: provides relational database and SQL skills for structured organisational information

courses.name: Algorithms & Data Structures
courses.actualContent: This course aims to provide the student with knowledge, skills and critical thinking ability in algorithm design and analysis. Inappropriate choice of algorithm and associated data structure can seriously impact on the performance of an application. The st udy of algorithm design and analysis provides techniques which help minimize the execution time of an algorithm. An emphasis is on the experimental performance analysis of algorithms. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Larger algorithm projects are also undertaken. There is a written midterm exam and a written final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained an understanding of how algorithms have helped shape the modern world.
courses.contribution: develops algorithmic problem-solving and data structures needed for computational business applications

courses.name: Introduction to Data Science
courses.actualContent: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
courses.contribution: develops data cleaning, visualisation and manipulation for evidence-based business analysis

courses.name: Machine Learning
courses.actualContent: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.
courses.contribution: introduces machine-learning models for prediction and analysis of real datasets

courses.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
courses.actualContent: Neural networks have enabled major advances in areas such as computer vision, large language models, and generative AI. This course focuses on the underlying theory as well as practical implementations in the Python programming language using packages such as TensorFlow . No familiarity with Python is assumed, but a willingness to learn and write code in Python is essential. In the first part of the course, w e start by building and training our own basic neural networks from scratch. We also use TensorFlow to create bigger networks and apply them to tabular data. In the second part of the course, we move on to more complex neural networks for applications such as computer vision and text classification . We also discuss recent developments in large language models (such as ChatGPT) . Finally, if time per mits, we have a brief look at image generation models (such as DALL-E).
courses.contribution: develops neural-network and deep-learning methods for advanced AI applications

courses.name: Introduction to Programming
courses.actualContent: This is the gateway course of Computer Science and AI studies; an introductory course in problem solving and computer programming in Python. The course begins by introducing traditional structured programming and data constructs (i.e. branching, loops, functions; tuples and lists). Then consideration is given to testing and debugging and finally the object- oriented programming constructs. During the entire semester, elements of discrete mathematics (e.g., logic, sets, enumeration) as well as certain computational problem solving techniques are also incorporated into the course material. There are classes twice a week. The first half of each class is a lecture where we learn new material, while the second half is devoted to laboratory work where students tackle programming exercises and demonstrate their work. Homework comprises weekly programming exercises and online quizzes. Two larger programming projects are undertaken. There is a written Midterm exam and a written Final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with the Python programming language as well as important concepts of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving techniques.
courses.contribution: provides programming foundations for computational and AI-oriented business work

courses.name: Mathematical Methods
courses.actualContent: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3
courses.contribution: provides mathematical foundations for quantitative and data-driven modelling

courses.name: Linear Algebra
courses.actualContent: Linear algebra is the study of systems of linear equations and linear functions. Systematic methods exist to solve such systems of linear equations. Matrices and vectors are introduced as the equivalent of a system of linear equations. This equivalence allows for reducing problems involving linear combinations of vectors to questions about systems of linear equations. The spanning of a (sub)space, linear independence and linear transformations are fundamental concepts in linear algebra. Matrix operations and theorems involving matrices will provide the basic tools for handling many applications of linear algebra. The invertible matrix theorem is a theorem of particular importance. The determinant of a matrix is an important scalar quantity related to the invertibility criterion for square matrices. Furthermore, the determinant is a measure for the amount by which a linear transformation changes the area of a ﬁgure. In multi-variable calculus, this measure is deﬁned as the Jacobian of a transformation. Introducing the more abstract concept of vector spaces allows for further generalization of these ideas. Many vector spaces resemble the well-known vector space Rn. In this course, the theory of vector spaces will be applied to the processing of discrete signals (Fourier Series), diﬀerence equations and Markov chains. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are used to understand the action of a linear transformation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors arise naturally in diﬀerent areas of physics and mathematics.
courses.contribution: Specific complementary foundation: matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations support the quantitative modelling used by the AI strand.

courses.name: Probability & Statistics
courses.actualContent: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
courses.contribution: provides probability, statistical inference and simulation foundations for risk and analytics

courses.name: Social Psychology
courses.actualContent: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
courses.contribution: provides scientific analysis of social influence, group behaviour and interpersonal processes relevant to organisations and customers

courses.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
courses.actualContent: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. courses.contribution: develops persuasive written and spoken communication for organisational and stakeholder contexts
